title: Tile the Floor

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (broken profile DP for domino tilings)

statement:
A floor is an `n` by `m` grid. A cell marked `#` is a pillar and cannot be tiled; a cell marked `.` must be covered. You have an unlimited supply of **dominoes** of size `1 x 2` that can be placed horizontally or vertically (two dominoes that cover the same cells in the same way are the same tiling). Count the ways to cover **every `.` cell exactly once** with dominoes that avoid the pillars, modulo `1 000 000 007`.

**Input.** The first line holds `n` and `m`. Then `n` lines of `m` characters each.

**Output.** The number of tilings modulo `10^9 + 7` (it is `1` when there are no `.` cells and `0` when it is impossible).
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100, 1 ≤ m ≤ 8 in this browser version (the idea scales to m up to 12 to 14)
hints: Placing dominoes one at a time and backtracking explores a number of tilings that grows exponentially with the area. Count tilings with a DP instead, scanning cells in order.

Scan the cells row by row. When you reach a cell, the only information from the past that matters is which of the next m cells (the rest of this row and the start of the next) are already covered by dominoes placed earlier. That is an m-bit mask.

At cell (i, j): if its bit is set, clear it and move on. Otherwise place a vertical domino (set the bit for the cell below) or a horizontal one (set the bit for the next cell in the row), if the cells are free. A pillar needs nothing. The answer is the number of ways to finish with an empty mask.
editorial: Process the cells in row-major order and keep a **broken profile**: a bitmask of `m` bits in which bit `j` tells whether the cell that the scan will reach next in column `j` is already covered (for columns before the current one this is the cell in the next row, for columns from the current one on it is the cell in the current row). The state after finishing a cell is `dp[mask]`, the number of ways to cover everything before it consistently with that mask. At cell `(i, j)`: if bit `j` is set, the cell is already covered by a vertical domino from above or a horizontal one from the left: clear the bit (the cell below is not covered by anything so far) and continue. If the cell is a pillar and its bit is clear, nothing happens. Otherwise the cell must be covered by a new domino: a **vertical** one, if the cell below exists and is free, sets bit `j` (now meaning that the cell below is covered); a **horizontal** one, if the next cell in the row exists, is free and its bit is clear, sets bit `j + 1` (the next cell is covered; bit `j` stays clear). A domino is never allowed on a pillar. After all `n * m` cells the profile must be empty, so the answer is `dp[0]`. There are `n * m` cells and `2^m` masks with at most two transitions each: `O(n * m * 2^m)`, which is why the narrow side is made the mask. Take the counts modulo `10^9 + 7` after every addition. Compared with row-by-row transitions between whole masks, the cell-by-cell form has constant transitions per state and is simpler to get right.

starter.python:
import sys

MOD = 10**9 + 7
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, m = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
grid = data[2:2 + n]

solutions.python:
import sys

MOD = 10**9 + 7
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n, m = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
grid = data[2:2 + n]
# dp[mask]: ways so far; bit j of the mask says whether the cell in column j at the current frontier is already covered
dp = [0] * (1 << m)
dp[0] = 1
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(m):
        nd = [0] * (1 << m)
        for mask in range(1 << m):
            ways = dp[mask]
            if not ways:
                continue
            if (mask >> j) & 1:                                   # covered by a domino from above or from the left
                nd[mask ^ (1 << j)] = (nd[mask ^ (1 << j)] + ways) % MOD
            elif grid[i][j] == '#':                               # a blocked cell needs nothing
                nd[mask] = (nd[mask] + ways) % MOD
            else:
                if i + 1 < n and grid[i + 1][j] == '.':           # vertical domino: also covers the cell below
                    nd[mask | (1 << j)] = (nd[mask | (1 << j)] + ways) % MOD
                if j + 1 < m and grid[i][j + 1] == '.' and not (mask >> (j + 1)) & 1:   # horizontal domino
                    nd[mask | (1 << (j + 1))] = (nd[mask | (1 << (j + 1))] + ways) % MOD
        dp = nd
print(dp[0])
